Posted July 22, 2005
Analysis by Richard Cowan

When I heard that the beautiful little city of Santa Cruz was honoring Wo/Mens Alliance for Medical Marijuana (WAMM) and its founders Valeria and Mike Corral last Saturday, I felt that I had to be there, and I was very glad that I could join in. They are really wonderful people.

Valerie asked me to speak about the death of Steve McWilliams, the San Diego medical cannabis activist.
See
 The Murder of Steve McWilliams  An Indictment, Not An Obituary. The Absurdity of Evil. Condolences from NORML.  

As I watched a series of Santa Cruz officials get up to speak in praise of the work being done by WAMM, it was hard not to think of the contrast with San Diego where the implementation of Prop 215 has been resisted by local officials in clear violation of the states Constitution.
From 1999, see
 Santa Cruz Shows Support For Hemp Expo By Agreeing to Close Street For Four Days; Now That Is Mainstream!

Hundreds of people, including many patients carrying plants, marched a few blocks to the cheers of the people. A group of patients in wheelchairs, including famed author Robert Anton Wilson, led the way. 

WAMM has been described as the perfect implementation of the spirit and letter of Prop 215, but that did not spare it from being raided by the DEA.
See pictures http://www.marijuana-art.com/ARaid2.html and http://www.marijuana-art.com/ARaid3.html

In September of 2002, DEA agents raided WAMM and cut down plants its members had grown for their own use. Suzanne Pheil, a partially paralyzed post-polio patient was handcuffed in her bed by the DEA. DEA spokesman Richard Meyer said, (W)e see them as victims of their traffickers.

Pheil responded,  "We are not the victims of drug traffickers - we are victims of the DEA. With a gun to my head the DEA stole the medicine that over 250 sick and dying people worked to grow."
See
 The Police Fraud. Someone Is Lying. Marking The 30th Anniversary Of An Article in National Review. What if Don Quixote Was Right? Analysis by Richard Cowan

No charges were filed as a result of the 2002 raid, but the Feds can strike again at any time and combine the number of plants from the 2002 raid with whatever they get at a later date. That was the game they played to federalize Steve McWilliams case.

I am hopeful that even the DEA will not try that with WAMM, because the 2002 raid was reportedly very unpopular inside the DEA and no federal attorney is going to want to prosecute such a case, but we are still talking about narks.

In Santa Cruz the sick, dying and disabled have the support of their community, and as a spokesperson for the local AIDS support group put it, we should not look upon Santa Cruz as an exception, but rather as an example of what America should and will be. I was reminded of Martin Luther King, Jr.s assurance that the civil rights movement would ultimately prevail because it did not seek to change Americas values but to challenge the country to live up to them. I think that the same is true of the cannabis reform movement, especially for medical cannabis.

The fact that the patients were carrying plants with them in the march and that was considered risky even in Santa Cruz shows how far we have come, and yet how far we have to go.

I have written about the problem of under-treatment of pain generally, about the great need for medical cannabis in the poorest countries.
See
 The UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs Resolution on the Control of Cannabis in Africa. UN Narks Urge War on Poorest of the Poor. Cannabis Prohibition Does Most Damage In Poor Countries.

The death of Steve McWilliams, like too many before him, was a reminder that people who live in pain should not have to live in fear, especially not in fear of those who claim to be helping them!
See
 What Is More Important, Prohibition Or The Patients? The Death of Cheryl Miller Should Remind Us All To Demand A Change In Priorities. Should Pain Be A Crime?
